Variance-prior decisions are often treated as a software detail. This tutorial reframes them as a sequence of transparent modeling decisions linking the target variance component, parameter scale, prior family, benchmark information, software implementation, checking, sensitivity analysis, and reporting.

## Abstract {#abstract}

This tutorial provides a practical workflow for specifying scalar variance-component priors in Bayesian multilevel models. It reviews gamma, inverse-gamma, half-*t*, and half-Cauchy priors and clarifies how prior meaning changes across variance, precision, and standard-deviation parameterizations. A worked TIMSS 2019 example uses benchmark information from a non-overlapping reference sample to construct alternative priors for a smaller target analysis. The emphasis is on making the rationale, translation, checking, and robustness of prior choices visible rather than treating any default as automatically neutral.

## Practical Workflow {#workflow}

The published tutorial organizes variance-prior construction into **five steps**:

::: {.workflow-list}
<div><span>01</span><strong>Identify the target variance components and implementation scale.</strong><p>Determine which variance component needs a prior and whether the estimation software specifies it on the variance, precision, or standard-deviation scale.</p></div>
<div><span>02</span><strong>Choose benchmark values and a level of prior informativeness.</strong><p>Anchor plausible magnitudes in prior evidence or a suitable reference sample, and make the intended prior concentration explicit.</p></div>
<div><span>03</span><strong>Calibrate priors on the variance or precision scale.</strong><p>Use gamma and inverse-gamma relationships to connect benchmark information to interpretable variance- or precision-scale specifications.</p></div>
<div><span>04</span><strong>Calibrate priors on the standard-deviation scale.</strong><p>Construct software-compatible specifications, including half-t and half-Cauchy alternatives, using an explicit calibration target such as a prior median.</p></div>
<div><span>05</span><strong>Inspect the implied prior, assess sensitivity, and report transparently.</strong><p>Evaluate prior densities, prior predictive implications, posterior comparisons, convergence, and sensitivity to reasonable alternative choices.</p></div>
:::

## Worked Example: TIMSS 2019

A two-level model of science achievement illustrates the workflow using a **non-overlapping reference sample** (7,408 students in 233 schools) and a smaller **worked-example sample** (400 students in 40 schools). The comparison examines priors for the between-school random-intercept and within-school residual standard deviations. Gamma, inverse-gamma, half-t, and half-Cauchy priors are calibrated to common benchmark medians on the standard-deviation scale and then evaluated using prior predictive checks, posterior comparisons, diagnostics, and sensitivity analysis.

## Practical Safeguards {#practical-safeguards}

::: {.mini-grid}
<div><strong>Prior-density inspection</strong><br><span>Check where mass is concentrated before fitting the target model.</span></div>
<div><strong>Prior predictive checks</strong><br><span>Ask whether the prior implies plausible data-generating behavior.</span></div>
<div><strong>Posterior comparison</strong><br><span>Compare conclusions under alternative defensible specifications.</span></div>
<div><strong>Transparent reporting</strong><br><span>Make the prior reconstructable by another analyst.</span></div>
:::

## Key Takeaways

- A numerical prior specification is not portable unless the **parameter scale and software parameterization** are also understood.
- Benchmark-informed calibration is most defensible when the source of information and its separation from the target analysis are explicit.
- Sensitivity analysis is part of prior specification, not a final cosmetic check.
- The goal is not to identify one universal prior family, but to make prior assumptions interpretable, inspectable, and reproducible.

## Contribution to my research program

This tutorial complements my simulation-based research on variance-prior performance by providing an applied workflow for calibrating, checking, and reporting priors across model parameterizations and software environments.
